extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science; informed general readers interested in American institutions and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the merits and defects of public opinion as a governing and supervising power in democratic (especially American) institutions, and how constitutional structure and social temperament affect its functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbounded freedom of discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every view and line of policy has its fair chance before the people; freedom of the press, public meeting, association, and agitation are widely exerted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no one is legally denied an audience, those whom the multitude condemns or ignores have no further court of appeal; under such conditions the sense of grievance that feeds resistance in persecuted minorities is absent. This condition contributes to the 'fatalistic temper' of accepting public judgment as final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intense faith in institutions / 'Mission of the Republic' belief
rubrics_metrics.description: A widespread American conviction in the soundness of institutions and a belief (often religiously expressed) that Providence or history favors the nation and will secure a happy issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This faith disposes citizens to optimism and submission: pessimism is the luxury of a few, and the individual tends to trust the multitude's honesty and good sense. It underpins reluctance to resist popular conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatalism of the multitude (individual acquiescence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of being one among a prodigious and uniform multitude makes individuals more ready to submit and less likely to resist majority judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include calmer reactions to everyday annoyances (late trains, delays) and a readiness to accept losses in private rights if public judgment has gone against them. The feeling that 'things will come out right' reduces personal protest and fuels obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion acquires solidity and removes issues from practical discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the masses have made up their minds on questions, those issues pass out of the practical region of discussion; controversy is confined to minor topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This solidity strengthens public order because individuals and small groups have learned to submit even when aggrieved. However, it can also mean that important underlying matters of agreement are not frequently reopened for deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of ascertaining genuine public opinion in an articulate society
rubrics_metrics.description: In a highly articulate population the sheer din of voices and numerous organs of opinion make it hard to determine which cry truly prevails or which represents many or few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press and many opinion organs often claim to speak for 'the people'; genuine opinion is surrounded by counterfeits. The one positive test is an election, but elections have limits in detecting subsidiary views and may be influenced by personal merits of candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of elections and referendums as measures of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections at best test division between major parties and leave subsidiary issues uncertain; referendums are logically preferable but costly and troublesome at large scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because elections come at fixed intervals and test chiefly party divisions, they may fail to show whether a particular opinion is gaining or losing ground or the voting strength its advocates can mobilize. Referendums are difficult to apply in federal matters and across large states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional balance can offload constructive work onto public opinion (lack of machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: By dividing and weakening single authorities (national vs state, executive vs legislature), the Constitution places on unorganized public opinion more work than it can discharge, producing a shortage of governmental machinery to translate desires into practical schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural dispersion means the people can express desires but lack mechanisms and leadership (cabinet-style or executive leadership) to convert ends into workable administrative or financial policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion can determine ends but is less fit to choose means
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion is competent to determine national ends but not always fit to examine and select the best means for achieving them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public sentiment is disposed to recognize broad and patent facts and obvious reasons; it is less adapted to systematic reasoning and the invention of administrative schemes. Historical problems (e.g., extension of slavery, currency, trusts) illustrate slow, clumsy handling of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: American legislatures often lack constructive skill and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are more like delegates responsible to local districts than councillors of the nation; legislatures sit short terms and lack executive leaders, reducing capacity for constructive legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the people desire concrete administrative schemes, legislatures frequently fail to prepare satisfactory bills due to want of leadership, timidity about going beyond opinion, and absence of skills in state legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion is slow and clumsy on large practical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion looks, talks, and complains incessantly about big problems but is often unable to grapple with or solve them promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because public opinion must gather and reconcile many local and class differences over a vast area, it moves slowly; vital decisions often hang fire longer than in European countries where cabinet leadership can act more decisively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of power helps fix responsibility; diffusion hinders it
rubrics_metrics.description: To supervise effectively and to punish dereliction, it must be easy to fix praise or blame on particular persons; divided powers make this difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free governments that concentrate power can fix responsibility more readily. The American division of powers makes it hard to apportion guilt for failures — people may rage but find no single victim. The governor's veto and stronger mayoral functions are cited as partial remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion's characteristic temper: heedless in small matters, indulgent
rubrics_metrics.description: Although quick on great matters, public opinion is often indulgent and neglectful of smaller evils, allowing many abuses to root until they become scandalous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chief difficulty for reformers is to catch and hold public attention; a busy or good-natured populace may tolerate particular jobbery until its cumulative effect creates a scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatalism and optimism produce indifference to mismanagement and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that 'things will come out right' and the individual's sense of insignificance lead citizens to tolerate incompetence and delegate corrective action to the multitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temperament partly explains long-suffering tolerance of officials' incompetence and mismanagement, and a lower personal sense of wrong compared to other national temperaments (e.g., English).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion chills leaders' initiative and dulls political responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Because leaders habitually worship and observe public opinion, they become less eager to propose original or unpopular ideas and more fearful of being labeled doctrinaire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical statesman in America tends to be timid in advocacy and infertile in suggestion; philosophy and historical study are needed as correctives to superstitions implanted by service to the multitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enormous force of public opinion risks national overconfidence and complacency
rubrics_metrics.description: Large freedom and success can lead a nation to mistake prosperity for greatness and to seek truth solely in majority voice, producing self-complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nation thus inclined requires 'prophets' or critical voices (instructed critics, philanthropic reformers) to rouse moral ideals and remind citizens of higher obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of instructed critics and philanthropic reformers in correcting public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructed critics (higher newspapers, literature) and philanthropic reformers (through churches) provide necessary irritation and critique to public complacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their influence is growing rather than ebbing; they help expose and combat evils and may in time extinguish corrupt practices that politicians perpetuate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity ('genius of universal publicity') as a check on abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread publicity and exposure are powerful in defeating selfishness, injustice, cruelty, and jobs of all sorts because 'selfishness, injustice, cruelty, tricks, and jobs of all sorts shun the light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No serious evils can long remain concealed; when disclosed they are half destroyed. This sunlight effect is one of public opinion's most wholesome outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation-level public opinion as competent determiner of national ends
rubrics_metrics.description: When the opinion of a united and tolerably homogeneous nation finally expresses itself, it is the most competent authority to determine the ends of national policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with some European practices where legislatures or cabinets may take decisions the nation had scarcely thought of and then disapprove; public opinion at the national level sets broadly legitimate ends even if it is imprecise on means.
